items.title: Iraq suffers nationwide blackout as war disrupts gas supplies

featured_image.name: Report: Blackout Hits Central, Southern Iraq

items.description: Iraq was plunged into darkness on Wednesday evening after a sudden drop in gas supplies at a major power plant triggered a cascading failure across the country's entire electricity grid. The blackout comes as Iraq finds itself caught between warring sides in the escalating conflict between the United States, Israel, and Iran.

items.title: US and European stocks rally as oil prices stabilize

featured_image.name: Stocks rally on Fed interest rate cut hopes as 'jobless ...

items.description:
U.S. and European equities rallied on Wednesday as oil prices paused their sharp climb, offering investors a reprieve after two days of market turmoil driven by the escalating conflict between the United States, Israel, and Iran. The S&P 500 rose 0.86%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 330 points, or 0.68%, and the Nasdaq Composite advanced 1.4%, according to CNN. In Europe, London's FTSE 100 rose 0.9%, Paris gained 1.1%, and Frankfurt climbed 1.5%.[1][2]

The rebound came after The New York Times reported that Iran had made indirect overtures to the United States about potential negotiations, and after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed to CNBC that the U.S. Navy is prepared to ensure "safe passage" for oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz "when it is appropriate and should it be needed".[3][1]

items.title: Iran has fired over 500 missiles and 2,000 drones, US military says

featured_image.name: Iran has fired more than 500 ballistic missiles, US military says - Yahoo

items.description: Iran has launched sweeping retaliatory missile and drone attacks against Israel, U.S. military installations, and Gulf Arab states, dramatically widening a conflict that began with coordinated U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iranian territory on February 28. Six American service members have been killed, dozens of civilians across the Gulf have been wounded, and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz has sent global energy markets into turmoil.

items.title: Israel vows to assassinate Khamenei's successor as son Mojtaba reportedly chosen

featured_image.name: Mojtaba, son of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, chosen as Iran's new ...

items.description:
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz issued an open threat on Wednesday to assassinate whoever succeeds Ayatollah Ali Khamenei as Iran's Supreme Leader, hours after reports emerged that Khamenei's son Mojtaba had been chosen for the role. "Any leader selected by the Iranian terror regime to continue leading the plan for Israel's destruction, threatening the United States, the free world and countries in the region, and suppressing the Iranian people, will be a certain target for assassination, no matter his name or where he hides," Katz wrote in a post on X.[1][2]

Katz said he had instructed the prime minister and the Israel Defense Forces "to prepare and act by all means" to carry out the mission as part of Israel's ongoing military operation against Iran.[3][4]

items.title: New study finds sea levels far higher than assumed, raising flood risk for millions

featured_image.name: Sea level rise threatens the North Sea coast more than expected

items.description: Sea levels along the world's coastlines are much higher than scientists previously assumed — more than 3 feet higher in some regions — according to new research that suggests tens of millions more people face flooding risks from climate change than earlier assessments indicated. The findings, reported widely on Tuesday, point to a fundamental flaw in the elevation data that has underpinned decades of sea level rise planning and research.[1][2][3]

items.title: 40 years of data reveal subtle shifts in the Sun's core

featured_image.name: Scientists detect changes deep inside the Sun during solar ...

items.description:
Researchers have found that the Sun's interior subtly shifts from one quiet period to the next, a discovery that could improve forecasts of solar storms and their effects on Earth.

A team from the University of Birmingham and Yale University analyzed more than 40 years of data from the Birmingham Solar-Oscillations Network (BiSON), a chain of six telescopes positioned around the globe, to compare conditions inside the Sun during four consecutive periods of low magnetic activity known as solar minima. Their results, published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, mark the first time scientists have used helioseismology — the study of sound waves trapped inside the Sun — to compare four successive minima side by side.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: US submarine sinks Iranian warship off Sri Lanka with torpedo

featured_image.name: Iranian warship sinks after apparent submarine attack near ...

items.description:
A United States Navy submarine torpedoed and sank the Iranian frigate IRIS Dena in the Indian Ocean off Sri Lanka's southern coast on Wednesday, in what US officials called the first sinking of an enemy vessel by torpedo since World War II.

US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth confirmed the strike during a Pentagon briefing, saying, "An American submarine sunk an Iranian warship that thought it was safe in international waters. Instead, it was sunk by a torpedo. Quiet death." Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Dan Caine said a single Mark 48 torpedo achieved "immediate effect, sending the warship to the bottom of the sea."[1][2]

At least 80 people were killed in the attack, according to Reuters, with 101 still missing from the vessel's 180-member crew. Sri Lankan forces rescued 32 sailors and transported them to Karapitiya Teaching Hospital in the southern port city of Galle, where one was reported in critical condition and seven others were receiving emergency treatment.[3][4][5]

items.title: Kuwaiti F/A-18 pilot fired 3 missiles that downed U.S. F-15s, reports say

featured_image.name: A Kuwaiti F/A-18 fighter jet was responsible for shooting ...

items.description:
A single Kuwaiti F/A-18 fighter jet fired three missiles that brought down three U.S. Air Force F-15E Strike Eagles over Kuwait on Sunday, according to The Wall Street Journal, citing three people familiar with initial reports of the incident. All six American crew members ejected safely and are in stable condition.[1][2][3]

The friendly fire episode, which occurred at 11:03 p.m. ET on March 1 during the third day of the U.S. war against Iran, marks the first loss of American aircraft since Operation Epic Fury began on Feb. 28. One F/A-18 pilot launched all three missiles at the American planes, according to a U.S. official. Air & Space Forces Magazine reported that surface-to-air fire is no longer the leading theory, contradicting U.S. Central Command's initial statement that the jets "were mistakenly shot down by Kuwaiti air defenses".[4][2][3]

items.title: European stocks post biggest gain since May on Iran diplomacy hopes

featured_image.name: U.S. stocks rebound from sharp losses, while oil prices leap ... - PBS

items.description:
European stocks staged their strongest rally in months on Wednesday as hopes grew for a swift resolution to the U.S.-Iran conflict, while oil prices pulled back from their sharpest weekly gains in over a year after President Donald Trump moved to secure shipping through a critical energy chokepoint.

The Stoxx Europe 600 rose 1.6% by early afternoon in London, according to Bloomberg, its biggest gain since May, after suffering nearly 5% in losses over the prior two sessions. The Euro Stoxx 50 climbed 1.6%, while U.S. stock futures pointed to a modestly higher open on Wall Street. Technology, utilities, and consumer stocks led the European advance, with ASML gaining 1.5% and SAP rising 1.6%.[1][2][3]

items.title: US sinks Iranian warship as strikes expand inland

featured_image.name: US strikes Iranian warship near Sri Lanka, over 100 missing

items.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine returned to the Pentagon podium Wednesday for their second briefing since Operation Epic Fury began, as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran entered its fifth day with no signs of abating. According to Reuters, officials said Iran is firing fewer missiles than at the outset of the conflict and that U.S. strikes would expand deeper into Iranian territory.[1]

The briefing came as the U.S. military disclosed it had struck an Iranian warship off the coast of Sri Lanka in the Indian Ocean, according to a Reuters exclusive citing three U.S. officials. The IRIS Dena, a 180-crew frigate, sank after what Sri Lankan defense sources described as a submarine attack, leaving at least 101 crew members missing and one confirmed dead. Sri Lanka's navy launched a rescue operation after receiving a distress call off the southern coast near Galle, with Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath telling parliament that at least 30 survivors had been pulled from the water. If confirmed as a submarine kill, it would mark the first time a submersible has sunk a warship in combat in decades.[2][3][4][5][6]

items.title: U.S. stock futures rise as oil steadies on fifth day of Iran conflict

featured_image.name: Oil surges for second day, Brent tops $83 after Iran orders Strait of Hormuz closure

items.description:
U.S. stock futures turned positive early Wednesday as oil prices steadied, offering a reprieve from days of turbulence triggered by the U.S.-Israeli military strikes on Iran that began Saturday, February 28. The S&P 500 futures pointed to gains at the open, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average and Nasdaq Composite futures also climbed, according to The Wall Street Journal, which reported that both futures and oil prices were stabilizing as the conflict entered its fifth day.[1]

The tentative calm followed a pivotal move by President Donald Trump on Tuesday, who announced the U.S. would offer political risk insurance through the Development Finance Corporation and deploy the Navy to escort tankers through the Strait of Hormuz "if necessary," according to Bloomberg. "Regardless of circumstances, the United States will guarantee the UNINTERRUPTED FLOW of ENERGY to the WORLD," Trump wrote on Truth Social. The announcement helped cap a sharp rally in crude prices, with Brent briefly topping $85 per barrel before settling lower on Tuesday.[2][3][4]

items.title: NATO destroys Iranian missile heading toward Turkey

featured_image.name: NATO defence systems intercept Iranian attack targeting Turkey

items.description:
NATO air and missile defense systems destroyed a ballistic missile fired from Iran toward Turkish airspace on Wednesday, Turkey's defense ministry announced, marking the first time a NATO member has been directly targeted in the six-day-old US-Israeli war against Iran. The missile, which traveled through Iraqi and Syrian airspace before being intercepted over the eastern Mediterranean, sent debris from the intercepting NATO missile falling into Turkey's southern Hatay province.[1][2][3]

The interception represents a dramatic shift in the conflict. Until Wednesday, Iran had deliberately avoided targeting Turkey despite the presence of US forces at multiple sensitive installations on Turkish soil, including the Incirlik air base near Adana and the Kurecik early-warning radar station.[4][5]

items.title: Greenland's fishermen face a crisis as warming Arctic melts the sea ice they depend on

featured_image.name: 'It's too warm': Greenland's fishermen are under threat from climate change

items.description:
Fisherman Helgi Áargil no longer knows what to expect on Greenland's fjords. Last year, his boat got stuck in ice that calved from a nearby glacier. This year, it has been unusually wet. His income swings between roughly 100,000 Danish kroner (about $15,700) per outing and nothing at all, according to reporting by the Associated Press from Ilulissat, Greenland.[1]

The Arctic is warming faster than any other region on the planet, and the consequences for Greenland's fishing-dependent economy are becoming harder to ignore. Fishing accounts for up to 95% of the territory's exports, with China, the United States, Japan, and Europe among the top markets.[2][1]
